term: "Vector Embedding"

## Simple explanation

A vector embedding turns an item such as a word, image, or passage into a list
of numbers. A model learns these numbers so that useful relationships between
items can be represented geometrically.

## Technical explanation

An embedding is a mapping from discrete or structured inputs to a continuous
vector space. Its training objective determines which relationships the
geometry captures: a text embedding trained for semantic similarity may place
paraphrases close together, while a recommendation embedding may encode
user-item preference patterns.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Embeddings make unstructured or categorical information usable by models and
similarity-search systems. Their quality depends on the training objective,
data, model version, and intended use; embedding drift can affect retrieval
quality after model or corpus updates.

## How it works

An encoder processes an input and emits a fixed-length vector. Downstream
systems may normalize it, compare it with other vectors, or use it as model
input. Production systems should record the encoder version and keep query and
indexed vectors compatible.

## Practical example

Encode each support article into a vector, then compare a user question with
those vectors to find candidate articles. Evaluate retrieved results on real
queries rather than assuming that a high similarity score means the article is
correct.

## Common misconceptions

- Embeddings do not have universally meaningful dimensions; individual
  coordinates are usually not interpretable on their own.
- Similarity between vectors is only meaningful within a compatible space and
  under an appropriate metric.
